summary:
NASA has burned things in microgravity for decades, and the results sit in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database: 24 combustion investigations and close to 2,000 tests. We built Flamy so that someone designing a spacecraft, a station or a Moon base can find the ones that matter to them.

You start by picking your crew environment and adjusting oxygen, pressure, fuel and air flow. A chart plots NASA's tests and highlights those run in your conditions. The investigations are then ranked, and each rank comes with its reasons, which answers the first objective of the challenge. The matching tests can be downloaded as a CSV file for anyone who wants to feed a flammability model, the second objective. For the third, each record states what the experiment measured, and where NASA files it under prevention, detection or suppression we say so. A Compare page puts two investigations side by side when they share hardware or when NASA links them. The built-in assistant answers questions using only these records.

We added nothing to NASA's data. When a value was not recorded, the site says it is missing.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flamy is a website with three pages. On Home you pick a crew environment (Earth as a reference, station and spacecraft, or Moon base and rover) and move sliders for oxygen, pressure and air flow. A chart shows NASA's tests with the ones that fall in your conditions circled, and two counters tell you how many tests and investigations match. Below, a card lists what NASA's data does not cover for your case, followed by the three investigations that fit best. The Investigations page ranks all 24 and opens the full record of each one, with a table of its tests that you can download as CSV. The Compare page takes two investigations and lays them next to each other: NASA's description, the ranges each one tested, the fuels, the instruments. A small assistant sits in the corner of every page and answers questions from the same records.

Behind the pages there is one set of tables built from NASA's PSI database (24 investigations, 1,989 test rows). Every page reads them through the same functions, so a number is the same wherever it appears.

Benefits and intended impact

Flamy is made for researchers and engineers. An engineer who has to choose materials or an atmosphere for a habitat can check in a few minutes whether NASA has test data for those conditions. A researcher can see which investigations cover a question, compare them, and take the test rows away as a CSV file. We also wanted the gaps to be visible, because a missing experiment is useful information for whoever plans the next ones.

Tools

Python 3.12 with Streamlit for the site, pandas for the data and Plotly for the charts. The mascot is drawn with three.js. We used Git and GitHub, uv to manage the environment, pytest for about 400 automated tests, and AI coding agents to write code faster. The assistant calls a language model through an API. No special hardware, only our laptops.

How it is creative

PSI is organised by experiment. Flamy starts from the user's environment and works back to the experiments. The ranking shows its reasons instead of a bare score. Compare only offers pairs that NASA itself connects, through shared hardware (28 pairs) or a documented link (10 pairs), so the site does not suggest a pair it cannot justify.

What we considered

Our first rule was to add nothing to NASA's data. A value that was not recorded stays empty on the site. Where we had to make a choice ourselves, such as the weights of the ranking, the page says it is our judgement. We left Mars out as a selectable environment because the challenge statement gives no atmosphere for it and PSI has no partial-gravity tests yet, so it appears as a future feature. Since the audience is researchers and engineers, every figure on the site can be traced back to its NASA record.
